2F OurBigBook.com
The nonzero leading coefficients and distinct degrees make P0​,…,Pn−1​ a basis of the polynomials of degree at most n−1. Consequently the given orthogonality implies ∫ab​f(x)Q(x)dx=0 for every such polynomial Q.
If f has infinitely many distinct zeros in (a,b), there is nothing to prove. Otherwise suppose it has fewer than n. Among those zeros, list the sign-changing ones as t1​<⋯<tm​, with m<n, and put Q(x)=∏j=1m​(x−tj​), using Q=1 when m=0. On each interval between zeros, f has a fixed sign by continuity. Crossing a sign-changing zero flips both f and Q; crossing any other zero flips neither sign. Thus fQ has one constant sign wherever nonzero. Since f is not identically zero, continuity gives an open interval on which fQ is strictly of that sign. Hence its integral is nonzero, contrary to orthogonality to Q. Therefore f has at least n distinct zeros in (a,b). This is the reusable orthogonality forces many interior zeros argument.

⟨S(x),S(y)⟩=21​(∣S(x)∣2+∣S(y)∣2−∣S(x)−S(y)∣2)=⟨x,y⟩.

For a standard orthonormal basis e1​,e2​,e3​, put vi​=S(ei​). These three vectors are an orthonormal basis. Since ⟨S(x),vi​⟩=xi​, we have S(x)=∑i​xi​vi​=Qx for an orthogonal matrix Q. Thus
T(x)=Qx+b,QTQ=I,b=T(0),​

an affine map.
For a finite isometry group G, take c=∣G∣−1∑g∈G​g(0). An affine map preserves an affine average, so for any h∈G,
h(c)=∣G∣1​∑g∈G​h(g(0))=∣G∣1​∑g∈G​g(0)=c.

If the possible values have probabilities p1​,…,pN​, allowing zeros, the Shannon entropy in bits is H(X)=−∑i​pi​log2​pi​, with 0log2​0=0. Each term is nonnegative, so H≥0, with equality precisely when one value has probability one.
For the upper bound, prove first that logt≤t−1 for t>0: the function t−1−logt has derivative 1−1/t and its unique minimum, zero, at t=1. Let m be the number of positive probabilities. Applying this inequality to t=(Npi​)−1 gives
∑pi​>0​pi​logNpi​1​≤∑pi​>0​(N1​−pi​)=Nm​−1≤0.
(6)
The left side is H(X)log2−logN, proving
0≤H(X)≤log2​N.​
(7)
Equality at the maximum requires m=N and equality in every logarithmic inequality, so every pi​=1/N. Conversely the uniform distribution attains it. For N=1 the maximum and minimum coincide at zero.

6B OurBigBook.com
Continue in the bistable regime k>2. At s=0 the reaction function factors as f(g,0)=g(kg−1−g2)/(1+g2). Besides g=0, its positive equilibria are
g1​=2k−k2−4​​<1,g2​=2k+k2−4​​>1.​
(11)
At zero, fg​=−1, so it is stable. At a positive equilibrium, use k=(1+g2)/g to obtain fg​=(1−g2)/(1+g2). Therefore g1​ is unstable and g2​ stable. The sign of f is negative on (0,g1​), positive on (g1​,g2​) and negative beyond g2​; these signs determine the requested reaction-rate sketch.
The stationary points of f(g,0) obey (1+g2)2=2kg. For k>2 its smaller solution gc​<1 is the local minimum, and its larger solution lies above one and is the local maximum. Since increasing s translates the whole graph upward, the low and middle equilibria collide when
sc​=−f(gc​,0)=2gc​(1−gc2​)​,(1+gc2​)2=2kgc​.​
(12)
For s>sc​, both stationary values of f are positive, while f(g,s)→−∞ as g→∞; there is exactly one nonnegative equilibrium, on the descending high branch. At equality a double low equilibrium remains, so the uniqueness assertion requires strict exceedance.
For completeness, if the later positive-input request is considered for arbitrary k>0, the derivative is fg​=2kg/(1+g2)2−1. Its maximum is 9k/(83​)−1, attained at g=1/3​. For k≤83​/9, the reaction graph is decreasing and every s>0 already has a unique steady state, so take sc​=0. For k>83​/9, the smaller positive stationary point gives the same sc​=gc​(1−gc2​)/2; above it the graph crosses zero only on its final descending branch. Persistent robust switching after input is removed uses the previously assumed bistable regime k>2.
Starting near zero, raise s past sc​ and keep it there long enough for g to pass the unstable threshold and approach the high branch. Decrease s back to zero slowly, or after ensuring g>g1​. The trajectory then stays in the basin of the high stable equilibrium and ends at the displayed g2​. The persistent switched state is g2​=(k+k2−4​)/2. This is the saturating autocatalytic switch; the conclusion presupposes k>2 and enough forcing duration, not merely an arbitrarily short pulse of large amplitude.

For k=0, the first integral
E(x,y)=2y2​+2x2​−3x3​
(13)
has E˙=0. The equilibrium points are (0,0) and (1,0). The linearization has eigenvalues ±i at the origin and ±1 at (1,0). The origin is a center equilibrium: the sufficiently small positive level sets of E are closed curves, since its Hessian matrix there is positive-definite. The other equilibrium is a saddle equilibrium.
At the saddle, E=1/6, and the separatrix satisfies
y2=3(x−1)2(2x+1)​.
(14)
Its two branches with −1/2≤x≤1 form a homoclinic orbit through the saddle; its remaining branches extend to x>1. Inside the loop, the closed trajectories run clockwise: above the horizontal axis x˙=y>0. The saddle directions have slopes +1 and −1. Outside the loop there are unbounded trajectories. The left panel shows the closed orbits and all saddle branches.

ii OurBigBook.com
For general k, the same energy gives E˙=−ky2. For k=0.1 the eigenvalues at the origin are −0.05±i3.99​/2, so it is a stable focus. At (1,0) they are (−0.1±4.01​)/2, so it remains a saddle equilibrium. The vector field has constant divergence −0.1: there are no periodic orbits, by the planar divergence criterion. Nor can the former homoclinic orbit survive, since E strictly decreases along every nonconstant orbit except at isolated crossings of y=0.
The stable manifold of the saddle separates escape to positive x from convergence to the origin. Its two branches approach the saddle in forward time with tangent slope (−0.1−4.01​)/2. The left unstable branch spirals into the origin, whereas the right unstable branch escapes. The shaded component on the origin's side of the stable manifold in the right panel is the basin of attraction. The boundary itself is excluded: its trajectories converge to the saddle. This boundary is the damped stable manifold, rather than the conservative energy contour. energy decrease prevents bounded recurrent motion, and every bounded orbit off the saddle's stable manifold consequently converges to the origin. The plotted manifold was obtained by integrating backwards from the saddle's stable eigendirection.

0<Rez<2.​

Use a keyhole contour about the positive real axis for wz−1/(1+w)2, taking 0<argw<2π. The circular arcs vanish in the indicated strip. The upper and lower banks contribute (1−e2πiz)F(z). δS=∫t1​t2​​∑i​(Lqi​​ηi​+Lq˙​i​​η˙​i​)dt=∫t1​t2​​∑i​(Lqi​​−dtd​Lq˙​i​​)ηi​dt.

Least action here means stationary action, not necessarily a global minimum. The conjugate momentum is pi​=Lq˙​i​​; a cyclic coordinate, Lqi​​=0, makes pi​ constant.
For the symmetric top, ψ and ϕ are cyclic. Thus
pψ​=I3​(ψ˙​+ϕ˙​cosθ)=I3​ω3​,pϕ​=I1​ϕ˙​sin2θ+I3​ω3​cosθ

are constant, and consequently so is ω3​. Conservation of energy from time-translation invariance also supplies the conserved energy

I1​θ¨=I1​ϕ˙​2sinθcosθ−I3​ω3​ϕ˙​sinθ−V′(θ).

In the nonrelativistic dilute regime, E(p)=mc2+p2/(2m)+⋯ and (mc2−μ)/kT≫1, so the Bose or Fermi correction in the denominator is negligible. The common Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution approximation gives
n≃h34πgs​​e(μ−mc2)/kT∫0∞​p2e−p2/(2mkT)dp.
(22)
Differentiating the quoted Gaussian integral with respect to its squared scale gives ∫0∞​p2e−ap2dp=π​/(4a3/2). Therefore
n=gs​(h22πmkT​)3/2e(μ−mc2)/kT.​
(23)
chemical equilibrium of p+n↔D requires μD​=μp​+μn​. Apply the density formula to each species to obtain
nn​np​nD​​=gn​gp​gD​​(h22πkT​)−3/2(mn​mp​mD​​)3/2eBD​/kT.
(24)
Using gn​=gp​=2, the specified gD​=4, and mn​≃mp​, mD​≃2mp​, gives
nn​np​nD​​≃(h2πmp​kT​)−3/2eBD​/kT.​
(25)
For Xa​=na​/nB​ and nB​=ηnγ​, the corresponding deuterium equilibrium abundance is
Xn​Xp​XD​​≃π​16ζ(3)​η(mp​c2kT​)3/2eBD​/kT.​
(26)
The very small baryon-to-photon ratio means that even the high-energy tail contains many photons per baryon capable of destroying deuterium when kT is of order BD​. Substantial deuterium survives only after that tail has been exponentially suppressed, so BD​/kT must be large enough to offset the small prefactor. This is the deuterium bottleneck, not a threshold set just by equality of thermal energy and binding energy. The degeneracy gD​=4 is used as stipulated for this calculation.

Solution

11G OurBigBook.com
inversion in a circle with center c and radius r>0 is I(z)=c+r2/(z−c), with c and infinity interchanged. It fixes the circle pointwise and reverses complex orientation. Each inversion is fractional-linear in z, so composing two eliminates the conjugation and gives (az+b)/(cz+d) with nonzero determinant: a Möbius transformation.
Translate and rotate two distinct centers to 0,d, where d>0, and let the radii be r,s. The composition of inversion in the first circle followed by the second is
T(z)=d+r2−dzs2z​.
(27)
Its fixed points solve dz2−(d2+r2−s2)z+dr2=0. The discriminant is
Δ=(d2−(r+s)2)(d2−(r−s)2).
(28)
Disjoint circle boundaries require either d>r+s or d<∣r−s∣, so both factors have the same nonzero sign and Δ>0. There are two distinct fixed points on the line of centers. If the circles are concentric, their radii differ and the composition is z↦(s2/r2)z, with exactly the two fixed points 0,∞. Thus the composition has two distinct fixed points, also for nested disjoint circles. Reversing the order inverts the Möbius transformation and leaves its fixed points unchanged.

12G OurBigBook.com
For a binary symmetric channel with crossover probability p, Shannon's noisy coding theorem gives capacity C=1−h2​(p) bits per use, where h2​(p)=−plog2​p−(1−p)log2​(1−p). For any rate below capacity there are block codes with block length tending to infinity and decoding error tending to zero. Conversely, vanishing-error transmission cannot have asymptotic rate above capacity. At p=1/2 the capacity is zero; the formula also covers p>1/2 by complementing the output.
For discrete random variables, mutual information is
I(X;Y)=∑x,y​pxy​log2​px​py​pxy​​=H(X)+H(Y)−H(X,Y).
(29)
The formula is symmetric. To prove nonnegativity, apply logt≤t−1 to t=px​py​/pxy​ for positive joint masses. Multiplication by pxy​ and summation gives −Ilog2≤∑pxy​>0​px​py​−1≤0. Hence I≥0, with equality precisely for independence. The channel information capacity is suppX​​I(X;Y), over input distributions.
For the ternary channel every conditional output row has entropy hrow​=−(1−2β)log2​(1−2β)−2βlog2​β, independent of the input. Therefore I=H(Y)−hrow​≤log2​3−hrow​. Uniform input produces uniform output, since the matrix is doubly stochastic, and attains the bound. Thus
C=log2​3+(1−2β)log2​(1−2β)+2βlog2​β.​
(30)
Use 0log0=0 at the endpoints. At β=0 the noiseless capacity is log2​3; at β=1/3 all output rows are uniform and capacity is zero.

The array has K=10 replicates, I=2 levels of factor a, and J=3 levels of factor b, giving n=60. R vectorizes an array with the first index changing fastest, then the second, then the third. Accordingly, gl(I,K,length(y)) repeats each a level for the ten replicates and cycles over its two levels, while gl(J,K*I,length(y)) repeats each b level for twenty observations. These factors align with the vectorized response.
The first fit is the additive Analysis of variance model Ykij​=μ+αi​+βj​+εkij​, with independent normal errors of common variance σ2. Under the default treatment constraints α1​=β1​=0, the four fitted coefficients estimate the baseline cell mean, the a=2 minus a=1 effect, and the b=2,3 contrasts with b=1. Thus the baseline fitted mean is 3.7673, the second a level adds 3.4542, and the second and third b levels add −6.3215 and −5.8268.
The summary t tests compare each indicated coefficient with zero, using its standard error and residual variance estimate 77.20/56. They have 56 residual degrees of freedom. The three non-intercept contrasts are strongly significant; the intercept test asks whether the baseline mean is zero, not whether either factor matters overall. The Analysis of variance tests are joint nested-model F tests: no a main effect, with one numerator degree of freedom, and no b main effect, with two. Their sequential sums of squares are 178.98 and 494.39. In this balanced design the main-effect subspaces are orthogonal, so ordering a,b does not change those sums of squares. The denominator is the same residual mean square 77.20/56; both factor effects are highly significant.
The second fit expands a*b to a+b+a:b, adding two interaction coefficients. It allows the a effect to differ between b levels and has six parameters, equivalently one mean per cell, with 54 residual degrees of freedom. The interaction adds only about 0.27 to explained sum of squares; its F statistic is 0.0963 with degrees of freedom (2,54) and p=0.9084. There is no evidence against additivity, so the simpler first model is preferable on these data. This does not prove the true interaction is exactly zero.
For the final expression, p=6, p0​=4, and n=60. The fitted vectors are orthogonal projections onto nested model spaces, so ∥PY−P0​Y∥2 is the additional sum of squares due to interaction. The final code computes
F=∥y−PY∥2/54∥PY−P0​Y∥2/2​=0.0963 approximately,​
(31)
the same interaction test as the Analysis of variance row. The exact value uses the original, unrounded observations and fits. Using only the displayed rounded sums 0.27 and 76.93 gives about 0.0948 instead; that discrepancy is rounding, not a different test. The omitted observations prevent reconstructing more digits from the printed data alone.

The chain rule gives zx​=sin2x, zx2​=4z(1−z), and zxx​=2(1−2z). Therefore
4z(1−z)wzz​+2(1−2z)wz​+n2w=0,
(32)
which, after division, is the printed equation. It has only three regular singular points, 0,1,∞, and is thus a Papperitz equation. At zero and one the indicial roots are 0,1/2. At infinity, inserting w∼z−ρ gives ρ=±n/2. Its Papperitz symbol is
P⎩⎨⎧​001/2​∞n/2−n/2​101/2​;z⎭⎬⎫​.​
(33)
The exponent sum is one, as required for a three-singularity second-order equation.
Multiplying the equation by z(1−z) puts it in Gauss hypergeometric equation form with a=n/2, b=−n/2, c=1/2. The solution analytic at zero and normalized to one is 2​F1​(a,b;c;z). Composing it with z=sin2x gives an even analytic solution of wxx​+n2w=0 with w(0)=1, wx​(0)=0. Uniqueness of this ordinary differential equation implies
2​F1​(n/2,−n/2;1/2;sin2x)=cosnx.​
(34)
This Gauss hypergeometric function identity initially holds near zero, and on ∣x∣<π/2 with the usual real branch; it extends by matching analytic continuation. It is not an identity on every real x if the left side is always reevaluated on its principal z branch: for n=1 that principal value is 1−sin2x​=∣cosx∣. Continuing the branch consistently restores the stated cosine.

Let a comoving test particle have physical radius R=a(t)χ, where χ is fixed. Assume Newtonian gravity, spherical homogeneity, negligible pressure, and no mass flux through this sphere, so its enclosed mass M=(4π/3)ρR3 is constant. The shell theorem gives a conserved specific energy

A well-order is a linearly ordered set in which every nonempty subset has a least element. First note that a well-order cannot be isomorphic to a proper initial segment of itself: the least element moved by such an isomorphism would have exactly the same predecessor set on each side, forcing it to be fixed. The same least-disagreement argument makes an isomorphism between initial segments unique.
Match a∈A to b∈B exactly when their strict predecessor sets are order-isomorphic. The preceding observation makes each match unique. Matches preserve order and fill initial segments on both sides, since restricting an isomorphism matches every earlier element. If both sides had an unmatched element, take the least unmatched a and b. Their predecessor sets would be exactly the already matched segments, so they too would match, a contradiction. Therefore the matching exhausts at least one well-order and gives an isomorphism of that whole set onto an initial segment of the other. Uniqueness follows from the same predecessor-set argument. The whole set is allowed as an initial segment; this includes equal order types.
For ordinal division, let β>0 and choose
γ=sup{η:βη≤α}.
(39)
This supremum is a set ordinal because βη≥η bounds the displayed ordinals by α. Strict increase and continuity of multiplication in the right argument imply βγ≤α<β(γ+1). Take the order type δ of the remaining tail of α after its initial segment of type βγ. Then α=βγ+δ; if δ≥β it would contradict the strict upper inequality. Thus
α=βγ+δ,δ<β.​
(40)
The half-open intervals [βη,β(η+1)) are disjoint, so γ is unique, and uniqueness of the tail gives uniqueness of δ. This is left-divisor ordinal division: the order of multiplication cannot be interchanged.
Apply it with β=ω. The remainder is finite. A nonzero remainder makes ωγ+δ a successor, while a nonzero ωγ is a limit: for successor γ it ends in a full block of type ω, and for limit γ it is the supremum of the earlier blocks. Consequently
λ=0 is a limit ordinal⟺λ=ωγ for some γ>0.​

Euler characteristic for a finite connected plane graph is v−e+f=2. For a simple connected planar graph with v≥3, each facial boundary has length at least three and the total boundary length is 2e, so 3f≤2e. Combining gives e≤3v−6, and therefore average degree of a graph 2e/v<6. Some vertex has degree at most five. Components of size one or two have this property directly, so every nonempty finite simple planar graph has δ(G)≤5.
Prove five colour theorem by induction on vertex count. Remove a vertex x of degree at most five and colour the remaining planar graph with five colours. If its neighbours use fewer than five colours, assign an unused colour to x. Otherwise its five neighbours x1​,…,x5​ occur in cyclic order around x with colours 1,…,5. If no path of colours 1,3 connects x1​ to x3​, interchange these colours in the component of x1​, freeing colour 1 at x.
If such a path exists, a simple path together with xx1​ and xx3​ makes a Jordan curve. The cyclic order puts x2​ and x4​ on opposite sides. A path of colours 2,4 between them would have to cross the curve, impossible in the plane embedding; it cannot meet the differently coloured path or use the removed vertex. Interchange colours 2,4 in the component of x2​, freeing colour 2 at x. The colouring extends in every case. Thus χ(G)≤5 for finite simple planar graphs. The usual simple-graph convention is needed: loops would invalidate a proper-colouring assertion.

23H (Riemann Surfaces)

Words: 297 Articles: 1
Paper 1 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 297
23H OurBigBook.com
A Riemann surface is a connected one-complex-dimensional manifold with holomorphic chart transitions. A map between such surfaces is holomorphic when all its local coordinate expressions are holomorphic; it is biholomorphic when it is a bijection whose inverse is also holomorphic.
The open mapping theorem says a nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected complex domain maps open sets to open sets. Applied in charts, with the identity theorem excluding a locally constant portion, it makes a nonconstant holomorphic map of connected surfaces open. If the domain is compact, its image is compact and hence closed in the Hausdorff target. A nonempty set both open and closed in a connected target is the whole target. Therefore the map is surjective, without any appeal to degree.
For a biholomorphism ϕ:Δ∗→Δ∗, both ϕ and its inverse are bounded near the missing origin. They extend holomorphically across zero by removability: in a Laurent series a negative coefficient satisfies ∣a−m​∣≤Mrm on radius r, hence vanishes as r→0. Let the extensions be F,G. Their images lie in Δ: a modulus-one interior value would force a bounded holomorphic map to be constant by the maximum modulus principle. The compositions GF and FG equal the identity on the punctured disk and thus on the disk by continuity. If F(0)=0, then G(F(0)) would be nonzero because the original inverse maps Δ∗ into itself, contradicting G(F(0))=0. Consequently
F:Δ→Δ is biholomorphic and F(0)=0.​
(58)
For the final assertion only continuity on R and holomorphicity on R∖{p} are needed; the printed stronger description is redundant. Choose a target chart about f(p) and, by continuity, a small source chart mapped into it. The resulting scalar function is holomorphic on a punctured disk and bounded near its center, so the same Laurent argument removes its singularity. continuity makes the extension's central value equal the prescribed value. Thus f is holomorphic also at p.

The Lehmann–Scheffé theorem now proves the minimum-variance assertion. Failure to attain the Cramér–Rao bound does not disprove minimum variance within the class of unbiased estimators.
For the actual observations, the two likelihood functions are

They differ by a factor independent of λ. The likelihood principle consequently requires the same inferential conclusions, since the observed data carry proportional likelihoods. But the two minimum-variance unbiased estimates are 10/3 and 3​ respectively. Minimum-variance unbiased estimation therefore violates the likelihood principle: its unbiasedness and variance refer to the sampling plan, including the stopping rule, rather than solely to the observed Likelihood function.

A Hamiltonian system with n degrees of freedom is Liouville integrable if it has n functionally independent first integrals, including the Hamiltonian, whose pairwise Poisson brackets vanish. Functional independence is required on a regular open set. The Arnold-Liouville theorem says that a connected compact regular common level of these integrals is an n-torus, with a neighborhood admitting action-angle coordinates; the Hamiltonian flow there has constant angular velocities and fixed actions. Compactness is essential to the torus conclusion.
Use {f,g}=∑j​(fqj​​gpj​​−fpj​​gqj​​). On r>0, for differentiable F, Hamilton's equations give q˙​=p, p˙​=−F′(r)q/r. Hence the angular momentum M=q×p obeys
M˙=q˙​×p+q×p˙​=p×p−rF′(r)​q×q=0.
(88)
In particular M1​ and M2​ are first integrals. The Jacobi identity for the Poisson bracket is
{f,{g,h}}+{g,{h,f}}+{h,{f,g}}=0.
(89)
Taking f=H,g=M1​,h=M2​ shows {H,{M1​,M2​}}=0. Direct differentiation gives M3​={M1​,M2​}=q1​p2​−q2​p1​ and, cyclically, {Mi​,Mj​}=ϵijk​Mk​.
Set L2=M12​+M22​+M32​. Then {L2,M3​}=2M1​(−M2​)+2M2​M1​=0, and the brackets of H with both expressions vanish. Thus
H, L2, M3​ are three commuting first integrals.​
(90)
For functional independence, at q=(r,0,0) with r>0 the Jacobian matrix of (H,L2,M3​) with respect to (p1​,p2​,p3​) is
​p1​00​p2​2r2p2​r​p3​2r2p3​0​​,
(91)
whose determinant is −2r3p1​p3​. It is nonzero when p1​p3​=0. More generally this minor is a nonzero polynomial in q,p, independent of F, so its zero set has empty interior and the integrals are independent on a dense open regular set. This proves Liouville integrability on the regular set. The arbitrary potential in the question does not ensure compact common levels: F=0 has unbounded free trajectories. The full torus conclusion applies to those regular connected common levels which are compact, rather than to every choice of F and every level.

Linearity and symmetry under permutations of the axes force each diagonal entry to be λtre+2μeii​, with the same constants for each axis. Rotating back gives τij​=λekk​δij​+2μeij​. equality forces that row sum to equal one and every linked neighbor to attain the same maximum modulus. Propagate this along the connected axial grid to a boundary-adjacent row, whose row sum is strictly less than one, a contradiction. All eigenvalues therefore have modulus strictly below one. Hence Bk→0 and the Jacobi errors tend to zero from every initial vector. The unique solution exists by positive definiteness, so Jacobi converges for this discretization in any ordering.​
